unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Pathogens and infectious agents driving tumorigenesis, exemplified by EBV in Burkitt lymphoma
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Dietary carcinogens and the metabolic activation of fungal aflatoxin into mutagenic DNA adducts
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture shifts focus from infectious and viral agents to chemical carcinogens in food and their biochemical conversion into reactive mutagens.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 9 simply continues the ongoing survey of specific environmental carcinogens that began in subtopic 7, examining chemical mutagens alongside biological ones.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Dietary carcinogens and the metabolic activation of fungal aflatoxin into mutagenic DNA adducts
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: UV radiation causing DNA damage via the formation of thymine dimers
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture transitions from chemical and dietary mutagens to physical radiation as a direct cause of DNA damage.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 10 is a brief single-paragraph entry within the continuous walkthrough of environmental mutagens and DNA damage mechanisms.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: UV radiation causing DNA damage via the formation of thymine dimers
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke and meat, AhR signaling, and CYP1A1-mediated DNA adduct and ROS formation
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecturer introduces cigarette smoke and details the molecular xenobiotic metabolism pathway involving the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and CYP1A1.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 11 and 12 remain part of the overarching examination of environmental carcinogens and how endogenous metabolism converts inert compounds into active mutagens.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cigarette smoke and meat, AhR signaling, and CYP1A1-mediated DNA adduct and ROS formation
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Tissue-specific carcinogen activation illustrated by aromatic amines and bladder glucuronidase
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture takes up the distinct conceptual question of tissue specificity in chemical carcinogenesis.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 13 is an extension of the discussion on cigarette smoke constituents and metabolic activation mechanisms, continuing the same thematic run.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Tissue-specific carcinogen activation illustrated by aromatic amines and bladder glucuronidase
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Non-mutagenic carcinogens, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between tumor initiators and promoters in the Berenbaum model
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The lecture shifts fundamentally from direct DNA mutagens to non-mutagenic promoters like asbestos and TPA that stimulate proliferation and chronic inflammation.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopics 14-15 continue the comprehensive catalog of environmental cancer-causing mechanisms, which is subsequently summarized as a unified whole in subtopic 17.

unsureMarks.segmentBeforeIsAbout: Non-mutagenic carcinogens, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between tumor initiators and promoters in the Berenbaum model
unsureMarks.segmentAfterIsAbout: Host developmental timing and tissue proliferative state in susceptibility to carcinogenesis, followed by a summary of all carcinogen mechanisms
unsureMarks.caseForStart: The focus pivots from the properties of external carcinogens to host-specific factors, such as developmental stage and hormonal status during exposure.
unsureMarks.caseAgainst: Subtopic 16 completes the survey of factors influencing carcinogenesis, leading directly into the summary slide in subtopic 17 that synthesizes the entire section from subtopic 7 onward.

topics.label: Course introduction and lecture overview
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces herself, outlines the cancer lecture series, and presents the key learning objectives for the session.

topics.label: Cancer as a genetic and evolutionary disease
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the basic biological nature of cancer as an evolutionary process driven by acquired mutations, endogenous cellular processes, and genetic predispositions.

topics.label: Environmental exposures, public perceptions, and epidemiological evidence
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore common environmental carcinogen exposures, public understanding versus statistical reality, and global epidemiological variations in cancer incidence.

topics.label: Mechanisms of environmental carcinogenesis, tumor initiation, and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics systematically examine how infectious pathogens, dietary toxins, radiation, chemical carcinogens, non-mutagenic promoters, and developmental stages drive cancer formation.

topics.label: Methods for identifying mutational signatures and proving carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics describe the scientific approaches used to determine carcinogenicity, including whole-genome mutational signatures, epidemiological biobanks, in vivo animal models, and the in vitro Ames test.

topics.label: Lecture summary and risk-benefit considerations
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer concludes the session by summarizing key takeaways regarding environmental risk, carcinogen potency, and everyday risk-benefit decision-making.
